Good morning, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues. I hereby declare open the 19th meeting of the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council. Civic and political rights continue to be constrained by persistent patterns of repression, arbitrary detention, surveillance and website blocking. Undue restrictions on the rights of freedom of expression, of association and peaceful assembly, of the right to participate in public affairs are still in force. Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mozambique.

We believe that the promotion and protection of human rights are and should remain a priority for all States. Their implementation should not be politicized or pursued at the expense of State sovereignty, territorial integrity or independence. Instead, it should be guided by the principle enshrined in the Charter of the UN, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, international law, and international humanitarian law. In conclusion, we underscore that the consent of the states concerned is indispensable to the effective implementation of the mandate and mechanisms listed by the Human Rights Council. I thank you.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Burundi.

Burundi remains convinced that improving the human rights situation is a matter dear to the heart of all nations and therefore must be based on constructive cooperation and an inclusive dialogue between States. Sovereignty and territorial integrity of states must be a guiding light, understanding that the primacy of the responsibility of states when it comes to promoting and protecting human rights must be borne in mind. My country welcomes the commitment of Venezuela to actively cooperate with the Council and its mechanisms, and we can see this through the submission of national reports before the Human Rights Committee, the protection of the rights of migrant workers, the Committee on the Discrimination Against Women, and the Committee Against Racial Discrimination, which reflects its commitment to promote the well-being of its population. We also encourage it in its preparations for its next UPR which will occur at the beginning of 2027. And finally, my delegation encourages international solidarity and cooperation, granting priority to the initiatives of States on the promotion of human rights. Thank you.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Yemen.

Mr. President, you have the floor.

Once again, we call for an end to unilateral coercive measures, which seriously impact the living standards of citizens. It is essential to promote human rights through participative dialogue, technical cooperation, and ensuring that we have the consent of the states concerned, not by mechanisms which are imposed. All of this must be done without politicization. Thank you.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Switzerland.

Thank you, Vice-President. Switzerland commenced the investigative work of the mission and we thank it for its report. We call for the freeing of all persons arbitrarily detained. We take a positive view of the loosening of the restrictions to freedom of expression and encourage the country to continue in this direction. We remain concerned, however, by... the mechanisms and laws and practices which continue to restrict civil space and to limit the full exercise of fundamental rights. We support the renewing of the mandate of the fact-finding missions and encourage Venezuela to grant it access to its territory. We also welcome the cooperation between Venezuela and the High Commissioner for Human Rights and would call on the authorities to guarantee the OHCHR office a presence and full operational access throughout the country. Vice President, Which reforms do you believe are indispensable and should be a priority to guarantee the independence of the judiciary? Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Iran reaffirms its principled position regarding country-specific mechanisms under item 4. This raises a serious question about equal treatment within the Council. We are also concerned about attempts to judge states based on particular political or governance models. Countries that make independent political and economic choices are often subjected to pressure through unilateral coercive measures, economic-specific resolutions, and additional monitoring mechanisms. Together, these measures can limit the ability of peoples to freely choose their political, economic, and social paths. Venezuela is a clear example. Its people should not have to face economic restrictions and additional international scrutiny for exercising their right to self-determination. Human rights should not be used to impose particular political or development model. The Council must respect the right to all peoples to choose their own path. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Germany.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Germany aligns itself with the EU statement. We thank the members of the fact-finding mission for the crucial work for the people of Venezuela. At the same time, serious and structural violations of human rights continue to take place. Germany remains deeply concerned about the reports of arbitrary detention and forced disappearance, torture, and other forms of inhumane and degrading treatment. The remaining restrictions on civic and democratic space require the international community's continued attention. All arbitrarily detained prisoners must be immediately released and granted amnesty in line with international human rights law. Accountability is key for the people of Venezuela that have suffered far too long. Germany supports an extension of the mandate of the FFM on Venezuela for two years. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belarus.

At the outset,

Thank you.

Members of the fact-finding mission, what steps can the international community take to support civil society actors and prevent the shrinking of civic space in Venezuela? I thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia.

I thank you, Mr. Vice-President.

Thank you.

important confidence-building measures, including the release of political prisoners and the start of dialogue between the Venezuelan authorities and representatives

of the opposition.

We encourage the Venezuelan Government to continue

cooperating with OTHR, including by facilitating access to places of detention, and urge it to cooperate with the fact-finding mission.

of the Red Cross will be granted access to detention centers. The UK remains committed to supporting a peaceful, democratic transition that reflects the will of all Venezuelans.

Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sudan.

Thank you, Vice-President. We have listened very carefully and read the report on Venezuela and have taken good note of remarks made and recommendations. Thank you.

In choosing their own path of human rights development suited to national conditions to better promote and safeguard the human rights of their people.

Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt.

That is the appropriate way of ensuring that the human rights situation improves in countries and to ensure the cooperation of these countries with the Council's mechanisms. Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you, President. The FIDH and PREVEA denounce the fact that in Venezuela there is impunity for serious human rights violations and there is a repressive system which is responsible for persecuting civil society. The interim authorities are changing the legal framework to accommodate oil agreements with the Trump administration, but there's been the repeal of no laws arbitrarily used to detain thousands of Venezuelans, such as the law on hatred and that against NGOs. We have 300 political prisoners. Thousands of civil servants, pensioners and older persons have seen the real value of their income blown to smithereens. There are government vouchers for $200 a month, whereas the food basket is more than 700. Teachers are starting the school year without a real outlook of the consequences of the earthquakes earlier this summer. We have seen the repressive mechanisms of the state continue unabated. We need to guarantee the right to truth, justice, and reparation for victims and ensure there's a recovery of democracy and the rule of law in the country. We would urge the Council to renew the mandate of the mission. We would like to ask how you assess the role of the prosecutors and the ombudsman, given the current situation. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of Aula Abierta, intervention by video.

Distinguished members of Council, I'd like to share four ideas with you. And this is why academic researchers are prohibited from investigating the causes and solutions of electricity blackouts for eight hours a day, affecting millions of Venezuelans. This shows the link between academic freedom and economic, social and cultural rights. These are laws which must be repealed, taken off the statute books, not made more flexible. Secondly, the repressive mechanisms continue. The changes within the prosecution service and the ombudsman don't become truth, justice and reparation in practice. There are more than 400 political prisoners. The re-institutionalization implies that we'll have institutions which limit the exercise of power. Three, we must protect civil society as the agents of change and assess the importance of universities and researchers as key actors to rebuild the country. And four, we need the support of the international community. We need to renew the fact-finding mission with sufficient resources and a two-year operational program. Thank you.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to the representative of Amnesty International, intervention by video.

Mr. President, we welcome the FFM's new findings. Laws that seek to close civic space and control NGOs are still in effect. And as we speak today, around 400 people remain arbitrarily detained for political reasons. Amnesty International calls for their immediate release, for the closure of all criminal proceedings that remain open against thousands of victims of state repression, and for dismantling the repressive legal architecture, including the anti-NGO law. Mr. President, truth, justice, reparations, and guarantees of non-recurrence continue being absent. We remind authorities that these rights must be front and center in their actions. Here too, the FFM plays a crucial role. Its informed recommendations offer this Council and the international community a measurable roadmap for a future where human rights and the rule of law are protected in Venezuela. The FFM's mandate must be renewed for these and other valuable reasons. Given the FFM's findings on crimes against humanity in Venezuela, what are the options to preserve evidence for potential prosecutions?

Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of International Commission of Jurists.

Mr. Vice President, the International Commission of Jurists welcomes the work of the FFM on Venezuela and the reaffirmation of the persistence of human rights violations. We condemn the continued arbitrary detention of over 400 people for political reasons, in spite of the amnesty law. The announced reform of the Supreme Court and the justice system is vulnerable to political manipulation by the authorities and lacks transparency. We deplore Venezuela's recent denunciation of the Rome Statute, further proof of the absence of any way to prosecute those responsible for crimes under international law. In a context where the Office of the High Commissioner has faced unwarranted obstacles to engage effectively, Despite an MOU, robust international oversight continues to be critical. Finally, the ICJ urges the Council to renew and strengthen the fact-finding mission as it remains an indispensable mechanism for documenting gross human rights violations and ensuring accountability for the victims. Thank you.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to the representative of CIVICUS in the intervention by video.

Yorman Acevedo served eight months of imprisonment because he commented on the detention of Nicolas Maduro and Celia Flores. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of Lawyers for Lawyers for a joint statement, intervention by video.

The report of the mission, which has documented repeated restrictions on the right to effective legal defence. In Venezuela, civic space continues to be significantly restricted. Despite the Amnesty Act, hundreds of people remain in prison on political grounds. Lawyers continue to face harassment and surveillance when they take on politically sensitive cases. Although we welcome the release of detained lawyers, restrictive measures remain, including prohibitions on leaving the country, whereas lawyers in exile cannot return due to detention warrants that are still valid. Similarly, the independence of lawyers' bars, associations continues to be undermined, whereas restrictions on civil society limit their ability to provide legal assistance. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of Center for Justice and International Law, intervention by video.

President, distinguished members of the Council, The report submitted by the Mission continues to confirm the existence of a judiciary that has no independence and which has been used as a tool for persecuting and which is incapable of investigating potential perpetrators of human rights violations. Institutional rebuilding must prevent the judiciary from being used once again as a tool for persecution. This requires genuine processes of purges and then selection of competent persons in a transparent manner, as established by the constitution and in keeping with international standards. In contexts where impunity remains, speaking of a possible transition to democracy and of economic progress without an independent judiciary is an empty promise. The judicial reform is not a technical option, it is a matter of ethical, institutional and social urgency. We call on this Council to renew the mandates of the Mission and of the Office of the High Commissioner and to ensure through this monitoring and international support for these processes so as to achieve effective democracy. Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of International Service for Human Rights, intervention by video.

Thank you.

Distinguished Vice-President, Excellencies, participants, In Nicaragua, eight years from the start of the crisis, the human rights situation is ever more concerning. The silence and fear within the population have taken root as a consequence of repression that has reached all sectors. The silencing of dissent and criticism has made it possible for a number of institutional and legislative changes to concentrate even further the power within the hands of the executive and the ruling party. Democratic checks have been weakened, condemning those who suffer human rights violations and abuses to institutional neglect because there is a lack of independent and effective remedies in the face of the abuse of power. This is what the report that I'm presenting today documents in keeping with resolution 58/18 of this Council on the human rights situation in Nicaragua between the 15th of June 2025 and the 15th of June of this year. The legal reform approved in August 2025 made monitoring bodies subordinate to the authority of the president, granting the president's office the ability to appoint the prosecutor general, Further confirming this gradual weakening of the judiciary, there is no political pluralism in national institutions or at the local level any more. Out of 185 plenary votes in the National Assembly that were analysed during the period under review, not a single dissident voice was recorded, nor a single abstention, which casts doubt over the role of the National Assembly as a body for democratic deliberation. This same reality is visible at the local level too, where the governing party controls the country's 153 municipalities and both autonomous regional councils of the Caribbean coast. The latest constitutional reform, proposed and approved during the first legislature on 1 September of this year, deepens this trend. In addition to broadening the mandates of all the elected authorities and a number of high officials, it includes broad and imprecise prohibitions on political participation, which are likely to exclude any critical or opposing voices. Similarly, it establishes the non-applicability of international norms and decisions which are considered to run counter to national sovereignty, which could further worsen the lack of cooperation with human rights mechanisms. The shrinking of civic space is almost total now. During the period under review, civil society organizations recorded around 100 incidents against journalists, both within and outside of the country. These include surveillance, threats, smear campaigns, and police harassment. Moreover, one media outlet was closed down, and at least four organizations were also arbitrarily closed. Since 2018, at least 56 media outlets have been closed and 5,539 organisations have been shut down. Repression has also reached religious leaders and religions. At least 20 incidents of harassment have taken place against members of the Catholic Church. More than half of the Catholic dioceses remain without a bishop due to their bishops being in exile. General elections have been once again postponed until 2028. If the current situation continues, the necessary conditions for a genuinely free, inclusive and competitive electoral process will not be met. The arbitrary deprivation of liberty as a tool of repression against real or perceived opponents of the Government remains in place. In June 2026, civil society reported that 46 individuals were still arbitrarily deprived of their liberty. Our office managed to document 35 cases of arbitrary detentions, 29 of which present elements which could mean they could qualify as enforced disappearances. Particularly alarming is the increase in the number of deaths under state custody without there being any information about effective and independent investigations. Among the four victims that the Office documented, there is the indigenous leader from the Miskitu community, Brooklyn Rivera. The forced disappearance of relatives who then called for her remains to be provided show the risks that those who seek truth and justice face. The Office continues to document patterns of transnational repression which affect Nicaraguans abroad in exile. Because of fear and because of threats, some of them have been forced to leave their host countries. The Nicaraguan authorities continue to arbitrarily deny entry into the country of its citizens, as well as identity documents or the validation of academic qualifications. Indigenous peoples and people of African descent face specific risks which could jeopardize their physical and cultural survival. The mining activities supported by the state and new legal provisions are stripping them from some of their territories and their collective rights. Reports of violence against indigenous girls, including cases of kidnapping and acts of sexual violence, are particularly serious and require urgent attention. On gender equality, although the women still have a significant presence in certain fora of political representation, there are serious shortcomings when it comes to the prevention and punishment of gender-based violence. Civil society organizations have documented 53 femicides in 2025. Similarly, The restrictions that limit the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons remain in place, including reports of hate crime. Our Office would like to reiterate our call on the State of Nicaragua to release all persons who have been arbitrarily detained, to put an end to its repressive practices, and to resume cooperation with regional human rights mechanisms and with United Nations mechanisms. The Office calls on States who receive Nicaraguans to step up their efforts to protect them and provide support to the victims of human rights violations. In particular, we urge such countries to not extradite or expulse individuals who may be facing a risk of irreparable harm, and we encourage these countries to strengthen cooperation for investigating and cracking down on transnational repression. The international community must not ignore what is happening in Nicaragua. As has happened at other times during Central American history, the accumulation of diplomatic efforts from different countries, with the support of multilateral bodies, is necessary in order to re-establish the human rights of all Nicaraguans, so that they can freely participate in the destiny of their country.

If I'm sweating a little bit for the picture, please excuse me. Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen, it is my honor to present my report on transnational repression by the Russian Federation. Exporting the Rule of Fear Beyond Borders, the first ever country-specific report on transnational repression at the United Nations. In the past three years, before this Council, I have described the rule of fear inside Russia. Today, I report on how Russia is exporting that rule of fear. In preparing this report, I spoke with individuals followed and threatened abroad. with families used to coerce them from inside Russia, and with survivors of suspected poisonings. One of them is human rights defender Natalia Arnaout. She has said, "We should not lose vigilance. Even after leaving Russia, it does not forget about us." Honoured guests, transnational repression is not a series of isolated incidents. but the continuation beyond Russia's borders of the same structural, state-sponsored system of repression I have documented at home. Deliberate, institutionalized, and adaptive. Repression at home and aggression abroad are one policy. Transnational repression is where the two meet. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, between 650,000 and 900,000 people have left Russia. As civil society in exile grows, so does the machinery to pursue it. For direct physical attacks, the Russian Federation ranks third among 10 states responsible for over 70% of documented incidents worldwide over the past decade. Sentences in absentia rose from four in 2022 to 157 in 2025. My report draws on close to 400 documented cases of Russian transnational repression. The Russian Federation acts in three capacities: as perpetrator abroad, as the state whose listings and prosecutions others enforce, and as a host state enabling other governments. At least nine departments of the Federal Security Service are involved, with documented incidents worldwide, alongside military and foreign intelligence, prosecutors, and ministries. Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, the gravest form is targeted violence and threats to life. The Russian Federation has a long history of political assassinations, including the killing of Alexander Litvinenko with the radioactive isotope polonium-210 in London in 2006, former Chechen fighter A national of Georgia, Zelimkhan Kangashvili, was shot dead in Berlin in 2019 by a Russian operative whom German courts found to be acting on Russian government orders. Journalists and human rights defenders in exile have reported suspected poisonings too. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Russian Federation has become one of the most prolific perpetrators of transnational repression. Accountability is non-existent. Russian authorities deny involvement, at times promoting or honoring alleged perpetrators. For example, the first deputy head of the State Duma Committee on Security and Anti-Corruption, Andrei Lugovoy, was identified by UK authorities as the prime suspect in the 2006 polonium poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko in London. But Russia refused to extradite him to stand trial. He was instead elected a member of parliament. The defining change since 2022 is not only scale, but method. The repression now travels through arrest warrants, databases, banks, digital systems, and proxies, cheaper, scalable, and built to evade attribution. Forcible return is the most dangerous because it delivers the target into hands of the authorities from whom protection was sought. Torture survivor Mansur Mavlayev, a critic of the Chechen leadership, who fled Chechnya, twice attempted suicide, the second time on 15 September, after nearly 18 months in detention in Kazakhstan over a Russian extradition request. After repeated rejections of Mavlayev's asylum claim, he remains if returned at risk of torture or death. Yet, host states like Kazakhstan continue to honor legal assistance agreements with Russia, leaving victims in imminent danger. Others are not reached in time. Georgy Pirogov, a Russian national who had lived abroad since 2022, disappeared in Uzbekistan in 2024, resurfaced in a Moscow detention cell, and this July was sentenced to 23 years imprisonment on treason charges. Russian authorities have used such charges as foreign agent and undesirable designations, war censorship, law charges, and fabricated non-political charges to seek extradition of exiled dissidents to the Russian Federation and to place foreign nationals, including the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court and eight judges of that court, on international wanted lists. Police cooperation itself facilitates persecution. The Russian Federation is the most prolific user of Interpol Red Notices. Roughly half of the Russia-related cases reviewed by Interpol's oversight body in 2024 were found non-compliant with its constitution. The Commonwealth of Independent States wanted list has no equivalent screening or vetting procedure for politically motivated cases. None. Excellencies, repression now also travels through the international financial system. ROSFIN monitoring's register of terrorists and extremists contains 21,541 individuals. At least 5,063, nearly one in four, were prosecuted on politically motivated charges. Those designations are disseminated automatically and unvetted through global compliance databases enacted on banks without verification. private companies far from Russia effectuate Russian repression, often without knowing it. In June 2026, over the info, whose monitoring underpins international reporting, was itself placed on that register. That is reprisal against the evidence itself. By criminalizing its sources, the Russian Federation makes its own conduct harder to verify. Designations have also blocked independent Russian organizations from United Nations processes. The Russian government designated the Batani International Foundation as undesirable organization in relation for its engagement with United Nations Indigenous Rights Mechanisms. Reprisals of this kind reach into the work of this council. On 4 August 26, Federal Law No. 284-FZ authorized 14 categories of restrictions on listed persons abroad: assets freezes, passports, consular services, banking, property. They retain the duties of citizenship and lose most of its substance. My report calls this civic death, de facto statelessness for people who remain on paper citizens. Digital repression has become central. In early 2016, a campaign against secure messaging accounts compromised defenders, journalists, and more than 300 European politicians. Zarema Musaeva was taken from Nizhny Novgorod to Chechnya and imprisoned. The European Court of Human Rights found that her detention was retaliation for her son's activities. Weeks before she was seized, at least 37 of that family's relatives had been detained in Chechnya. When they cannot reach you, they target your mother. A designation made in Russia is not lifted by leaving Russia. The 2023 Supreme Court ruling on the international LGBT movement as an extremist organization follows people into exile, as do terrorism charges against indigenous people's advocates and women fleeing forced marriage and domestic violence in Chechnya. Selima Khadissova, who fled domestic violence, was detained on arrival in Bosnia and Herzegovina on a Russian red notice for terrorism. Bosnia and Herzegovina refused and granted her asylum. I must report again that the Russian authorities have not replied to my regular request for information or my repeated request to visit, and continue not to recognize this mandate. That refusal does not diminish their obligations. Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, transnational repression engages the obligations of both the originating state and the state on whose territory it takes place. Moreover, there is nothing inevitable about transnational repression. Where host states meet their obligations, it fails. Nevertheless, No binding international instrument specifically addresses transnational repression, and few states define the concept in domestic law. A dangerous protection gap thus exists in the absence of harmonized definitions, host state duties and frameworks for interstate cooperation, leaving victims exposed particularly to the bureaucratic, digital and low visibility forms of transnational repression that now prevail. Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the UN member states should elaborate a dedicated international human instrument, a binding United Nations convention on transnational repression with a monitoring and review mechanism, establishing a definition, provisions for prevention, accountability, and the responsibility of member states to close the protection gap. I call on this council to support the development of such a binding international instrument. I empathetically urge member states Treat transnational repression as a human rights issue, not solely as espionage or foreign interference. Comply strictly with non-refoulement and scrutinize Russian Interpol notices and wanted list entries. Require banks, compliance database providers, and their regulators to verify Russian designations and provide remedy. Protect and sustain funding for Russian independent media, human rights defenders, and civil society in exile. And protect exiled communities rather than securitize them. A response framed exclusively as national security and counterintelligence response turns victims of repression into suspects and leaves them unprotected. To the Russian Federation, I say, Seize all acts of transnational repression. Repeal federal law 284, the foreign agent, undesirable organization, and war censorship laws. End sentencing in absence and abuse of national security and public safety legislation, such as treason, espionage, counterterrorism, and extremism-related charges to silence dissent and anti-war expression, and placing victims of repression on terrorist and extremist registers, cooperate with this mandate. Excellencies and honored guests, the individuals in this report do not ask for privileged treatment. They ask for protection from forcible return to torture and sometimes death. the ability to speak, keep a bank account, hold a valid passport, and continue their human rights work in exile, and to telephone their mother without putting her in danger. Russian transnational repression is at once a violation of international human rights law and a challenge to host state sovereignty and the international legal order. It must be stopped. Mr. Vice-President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, I look forward to our interactive dialogue and to your questions. Thank you for your attention.

Thank you.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Romania.

Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ukraine.

Mr. President, Ukraine thanks the Special Rapporteur for her important report. Its findings expose a disturbing reality: Russia's repression doesn't stop at its borders. This connection is fundamental. Russia's aggression abroad and repression at home are mutually reinforced elements of the same policy. policy aimed at silencing dissent, suppressing anti-war voices, and spreading fear far beyond its territory. We are particularly concerned that Russia's security services monitor Russian dissidents, but also Ukrainians and other foreign nationals abroad, using infiltration, recruited specialists, and digital surveillance. The documented abuse of Interpol, extradition procedures, and international law enforcement cooperation is equally alarming, international mechanisms created to combat crime must never become instruments of political persecution. Madam Special Rapporteur, what concrete steps should States take to prevent Russia from misusing international law enforcement and financial institutions? Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Czechia.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. The Czech Republic aligns with the EU statement. We reaffirm our strong support for the Special Rapporteur's mandate and its renewal. The repression does not end when its victims leave the country. It extends beyond Russia's borders, seeking to deter human rights defenders from engaging governments, international institutions, and human rights mechanisms. Thank you.

I give the floor to the Distinguished Representative of Austria.

Thank you. Austria aligns itself with the EU statement and welcomes the report by the Special Rapporteur. Austria condemns the sharp rise in arbitrary arrests and detentions, the widespread and systematic use of torture and ill-treatment in custody, and the near total impunity enjoyed by perpetrators. We call for the immediate and unconditional release of all persons detained for peacefully exercising their fundamental freedoms. Austria also condemns the grave violations of human rights and international law committed by Russian forces in Ukraine, including the forcible transfer and deportation of Ukrainian children, and underscores that accountability for these violations is essential. Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of France.

Thank you, President. Since the start of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine, and more specifically over the course of the last year, the Russian authorities have stepped up their repression. France laments the designation by the Russian Supreme Court of the Memorial International Public Movement as an extremist movement. The prohibition of its activities in Russia, as well as the inclusion of OVD-Info on the list of "terrorist and extremist organizations," reflects the country's will to crack down on any criticism against the government. As your report documents in a very rigorous way, the Russian authorities are doing that most to reduce to silence their citizens, both at home and abroad, through physical violence, but also by instrumentalizing police and judicial cooperation mechanisms and by resorting in a systematic way to administrative retaliation measures and digital surveillance. Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Vice President, we would like to thank the Special Rapporteur for her report and her extensive work on the human rights situation in the Russian Federation. Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Poland.

Mr. Vice President, Madame Special Rapporteur, Poland aligns itself with the EU statement and wishes to thank Special Rapporteur Kacsohova for her report. Repressive legislation that criminalizes dissent, pervasive propaganda and disinformation, both in and outside of Russia, use of arbitrary detention, and widespread and systematic use of torture and ill treatment have created the unprecedented climate of fear and intimidation for civil society, activists, journalists, media workers, and political opponents in Russia. The scale of repressions starts to resemble the gloomiest times of the Soviet Union. Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

to target activists, journalists, human rights defenders and anti-war voices, including those in exile.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Montenegro.

It also increasingly relies on proxies to obscure attribution. Restriction on travel documents, consular, and banking services can lead to financial exclusion and even de facto statelessness. As the Special Rapporteur concludes, using international cooperation to assert criminal jurisdiction over the peaceful exercise of freedom of expression, association, and political participation in exile constitutes an impermissible assertion of extraterritorial criminal jurisdiction. Effective scrutiny, non-refoulement, and stronger safeguards are essential to prevent politically motivated measures for gaining effect through international cooperation. Yet, an effective response must fundamentally address its root cause. Depression within Russia, the systematic crackdown on civil society, human rights defenders, independent media, and critical voices must end, and all those arbitrarily detained must be released. Thank you.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Eritrea.

Thank you.
